title: The Unicorn, the Rat, and the Midnight Fair
markdown:
The house hummed like a settled blanket. Lily’s breath found its night-rhythm. In the moon-shaped nightlight, Pearl Decimal the unicorn toy lay still, horn smooth as a seashell, mane arranged as if sleep had rules. Beside her Almond, a plump rat the colour of toasted almonds, twitched whiskers and appeared asleep. Inside both, a different stillness: pine, moonlight, the idea of going.

“Did you hear that?” Pearl’s crispness, turned down.

“A badger’s tummy after grubs?”

“Something else. Rustling past the gate. Tiny feet on a playful breeze. A gathering. A secret one.”

Lily’s bedroom window overlooked the silver birch woods hugging the quiet lane. Tonight moonlight painted the familiar trees in shimmering silver and deep velvety indigo, mysterious and inviting. A faint excitement pulsed: something unusual just beyond reach. Pearl Decimal, ever sensible, straightened her already perfectly straight horn, a habit that always amused Almond. “If it is a gathering, it will require organisation. One cannot simply attend without a plan. I shall require my planning notes.”

Almond was already inching toward the window, paws barely sounding on the rug. “Planning notes? Pearl, it is night-time. For going, not for note-taking.” His eyes gleamed. Between organised unicorn and impulsive rat lived an unspoken theme: adventure might be the courage to notice simple wondrous things, not a binder of diagrams.

They wriggled from Lily’s sleeping hold. Pearl slid like a petal. Almond tumbled onto a sock. Together they nudged the latch. Creak. Cool fragrant air. The garden, by day balls and dolls, had hired shadows. Destination: the woods, and whatever was attempting a fair.

As they ventured past the creaky garden gate, the woods grew clearer. Twigs snapped under hurried paws. Leaves whispered dry. A low murmur — chirps, squeaks, rustles — filled the air. It was a gathering: a secret midnight fair. Squirrels chattered from branches. Field mice scurried with tiny seed-bundles. A wise-looking owl, high up, hooted a soft approving greeting. Woodland creatures of all sizes were attempting a fair with considerably more enthusiastic opinions than actual planning.

“Excuse me,” a tiny field mouse squeaked, struggling with a long brittle twig determined to snap. “Does anyone have a diagram for this stage? The brochure was rather vague, and this twig will not cooperate.”

Pearl stepped forward, pearly coat like a captured moonbeam. “A diagram is an excellent starting point. One must establish sturdiness, then appearance. I have devised a foolproof method for branch arrangement, based on the best way to hold weight. We shall categorise the branches by length and density.”

Almond, meanwhile, darted toward glowing insects, coaxing fireflies into a canopy. “Come on, little lights. Zigzag. Sparkle. Make it wonderful. Imagine a twinkling roof.” The fireflies preferred tag among the ferns, lights blinking in independent whimsical patterns.

Pearl, directing a makeshift stage of fallen branches, watched carefully balanced structures collapse with a disheartening clatter. Each time, a sigh. “Impossible.” She dusted pristine hooves. “My calculations were flawless. It must be an anomaly in the wood’s inherent structural instability.”

Almond, after coaxing and a few strategic sweet berries, got a few fireflies to blink in rough wobbly unison. The effect was less grand entrance than flickering Morse nobody could understand. “It is very efficient,” he told a nearby beetle, who shrugged its many shoulders.

Then Mr Quilliam the hedgehog, spectacles perpetually sliding as he peered at small print, bustled forward, brandishing a tattered leather-bound book. “Hold on.” His voice was stern and reedy. “According to the Woodland Fair Protocol Handbook, Section 7, Subsection B, all food distribution must commence with a formal tasting by the appointed committee. Entertainment must be preceded by a formal introduction, read from page 47, in a clear resonant voice.” The appointed committee seemed to consist solely of himself. The resonant voice was prone to cracking.

Pearl tried to implement a queue for the acorn-and-berry buffet, which was more heap than buffet. “Please form an orderly line.” Firm, polite, lost in the excited scuffle of paws and beaks.

The midnight fair was, to put it mildly, a glorious mess. The stage sagged dangerously. Fireflies blinked at random, a dizzying show more confusing than enchanting. The buffet was raided by more attendees than any queue allowed, a delightful unmanaged scatter of nuts and berries. Creatures who had started with bright eyes now grumbled softly; excitement faded like mist. The moon, high and bright moments ago, sat noticeably lower, casting longer melancholic shadows. The whole endeavour felt about to wilt before it had begun.

Mr Quilliam discovered something puzzling on page 47. “Good heavens. This is not fair protocol. This is a recipe for elderflower cordial. And a very delicious-sounding one.” Utterly bewildered. Spectacles askew.

Pearl felt a tight knot. Her perfectly straight horn felt heavy. Plans had failed spectacularly. Almond’s joyful leaps had gone awry too. The night felt like a soggy biscuit left in rain. The spark fading, last firefly winking out. A heavy silence. Damp earth and disappointment.

They huddled near a gurgling brook, water a dark inky ribbon. It carried little reflections of stars, diamonds tossed on velvet. Pearl sighed, silk on a quiet night. “It has all gone wrong, Almond. My organising was too strict. Your fun was too random. Neither worked.”

Almond nudged her, warm fur on smooth flank. “Maybe we tried too hard to make it exactly like a fair.” He thought of Lily, who never planned the garden perfectly and still found a dewdrop on a web, sunlight through oak.

Then his nose twitched. A subtle shift. A quiet invitation. “Pearl. Look.” Near where water lapped the mossy bank, a patch of clover, night-dew kissed, shimmered with inner light. He brushed it; a faint sweet scent rose, delicate, calming. A few steps away, late moon-daisies, petals like tiny silver saucers, caught the moon and pulsed with the night’s rhythm.

“And the brook,” Pearl exclaimed, finally looking away from disappointment. Her eyes widened. “Tiny reflections of the stars. A river of fallen constellations.”

Mr Quilliam, distracted from culinary crisis, peered at worn pages again. “This is not a protocol handbook. It is Mrs Higgins’s prize-winning recipe for shortbread. I misplaced my actual handbook when I moved burrows last spring. Wrong volume from the communal burrow library.”

A collective sigh, then relieved laughter, moved through the woodland. The pressure of a perfect fair, the confusion of nonexistent rules: a comical detour. Clover-scent, moon-daisies, starlit brook — the simple things. They shared the berries and acorns they had. Even Mr Quilliam, sheepish grin, offered shortbread knowledge, spectacles glinting. Nobody had butter. It was fine.

Pearl sat by the water and felt, for the first time, light without a checklist. Almond’s adventurous spirit had companionship instead of a collapsing stage. The woods’ quiet hum, daisies and brook-tinkle, was more than any spectacle they had failed to host. They had noticed the night that was already there.
characters: Pearl Decimal (unicorn toy who loves planning notes), Almond (a plump rat the colour of toasted almonds)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
